profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for an internal proposal to adopt ATRAF as the standard architecture evaluation approach within a platform engineering organization. The team has already drafted a 12-page design-review package describing how ATRAM would be used for product-specific systems, RATRAM for shared domain reference architectures, and AFTRAM for internal engineering frameworks such as service templates and deployment blueprints. The meeting is focused on reviewing whether the proposal is ready for approval for a pilot rollout in the IoT platform group, using a Remote Temperature Sensor-derived case study to demonstrate the process. The agenda is to review the evaluation flow, the pilot scope, the expected review artifacts, and the gating criteria for declaring the proposal 'ready'. The expected outcome is agreement on whether to approve the proposal with minor edits and what follow-up actions are needed before the pilot starts.

members.name: Priya Natarajan
members.expertise: software architecture evaluation, quality attributes, platform modernization, architecture governance
members.background: Priya leads architecture governance for the company's IoT platform and previously introduced ATAM-style reviews in several product teams; she is now sponsoring a lighter-weight, reusable evaluation approach for systems, reference architectures, and shared frameworks.
members.private_state: She wants the design review to end with approval for a pilot and is intentionally framing ATRAF as close enough to existing governance that no new committee process will be required; she is also concerned that if the process appears too heavy, product teams will resist adoption.
hidden_assumptions: When the proposal says the pilot will evaluate the 'RTS architecture stack', that naturally includes the concrete sensor service design, the domain reference architecture, and the internal framework conventions together as one connected package.

A design being 'ready for pilot' means the method, templates, and example walkthrough are sufficiently stable to run the first review, even if some scoring rubrics and training notes are completed afterward.

The 'risk register' in an architecture evaluation package is primarily a categorized list of sensitivities, tradeoffs, and follow-up risks captured during workshops, not a formally normalized compliance artifact.
The 'second spiral' in the iterative process is a lightweight follow-up pass using notes and revised scenarios after the first workshop, not a full second facilitated session with re-scoring.

members.name: Lucas Meyer
members.role: Senior Staff Engineer, Developer Experience and Frameworks
members.expertise: engineering frameworks, review automation, platform tooling, software process operationalization
members.background: Lucas owns the internal service framework and review tooling used by multiple product teams; he was invited because AFTRAM affects how shared frameworks will be reviewed and because his team may need to support templates and workflow integration.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid committing his team to open-ended process support and is listening for whether the proposal is concrete enough to automate in existing review tooling; he also wants any approved pilot to be narrow enough that framework teams are not dragged into product-architecture issues.
hidden_assumptions: When the proposal refers to the 'RTS architecture stack', it is using the RTS-derived reference architecture plus the framework layer as exemplars, not the product-specific system design itself.
A design being 'ready for pilot' means every artifact expected in the ongoing process is already specified to an operational level, including review fields, handoff rules, and closure criteria.
A 'risk register' should map each risk to owner, mitigation status, severity scale, and export format because it will eventually live in the standard engineering governance tool.
The 'second spiral' of ATRAF implies another formally scheduled review cycle with updated evidence, because otherwise the process is not repeatable enough to support consistent framework evaluations.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss using the 'RTS architecture stack' as the pilot example.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a single pilot package spanning all three levels together: the concrete RTS-inspired system architecture, its domain reference architecture, and the framework guidance layered above it.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the higher-level artifacts only: the RTS-derived reference architecture and framework guidance, with the concrete system design treated as background context rather than in-scope review material.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both think 'architecture stack' is a natural shorthand for layered architectural material, and in a design review it sounds helpfully comprehensive rather than ambiguous, so neither feels a need to enumerate exact boundaries.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly ask whether the proposal is 'ready for pilot' or 'ready to approve'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 uses 'ready' to mean conceptually sound and usable for a first guided pilot, with some operational details allowed to mature during the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 uses 'ready' to mean operationally complete enough that another team could run it predictably with the documented artifacts and workflow alone.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, 'ready' is a routine gate word that usually signals broad support; both assume the other shares their organization's common-sense threshold and do not restate explicit acceptance criteria.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the risk register
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to including a 'risk register' in the review package.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a workshop output capturing sensitivities, tradeoffs, open questions, and identified risks in a structured slide/table form for architectural reasoning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a tool-ready governance artifact with fixed fields, assigned owners, lifecycle state, and machine-ingestible formatting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'risk register' is standard across architecture and governance contexts, and both versions plausibly satisfy the same conversational purpose, so surface agreement feels complete.

misalignment_points.topic: How the second spiral will be executed
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the pilot should include a 'second spiral' after initial findings.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a lightweight follow-up pass by the same reviewers using revised scenarios and captured notes, mainly to confirm whether key risks changed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a distinct second review cycle with updated artifacts, formal re-entry into the workflow, and another scheduled evaluation session.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: ATRAF explicitly uses iterative spiral language, so both assume iteration is already understood; because they agree a second spiral is desirable, neither probes the mechanics of how formal that iteration must be.

turns.inner_thought: I need to frame this as an incremental extension of what governance already does, not a net-new approval machine. If we can leave today with agreement that ATRAF is ready for pilot, I can run the first review using the RTS architecture stack as the full connected package: the concrete sensor service design, the domain reference architecture, and the framework conventions together. Ready for pilot does not mean every scoring detail is frozen; it means the method, templates, and example walkthrough are stable enough to start and learn.
